translations.text: Hunger shall destroy one, storm shall drive one away, the spear shall destroy one, battle shall kill one.
One shall live his life without sight and grope with his hands. One, lame in the foot and sick with wounds in the sinews, shall lament his pain and mourn the decree of fate, troubled in mind.
One shall fall featherless from a high tree in the forest. He is in flight all the same, tossing in the air, until he is no longer the fruit [?] of the tree.
Then he sinks to the roots, darkened in spirit and robbed of his soul. He falls to the earth, and his spirit is on its journey.

One shall be forced to go on foot on distant ways and carry his provisions, treading the dewy track of foreign peoples and dangerous lands. He has few living people to support him. The friendless man is hated everywhere because of his misfortunes.
There the raven takes his eyesight, and the dark-coated one tears at the soulless body. Nor can he ward off that wicked deed with his hands, nor the hateful robber of the air.
His life has departed. Without feeling and without hope of life, pale on the gallows, he awaits his fate, wrapped in the mist of death. His name is accursed!

Fire shall torment one on the pyre. The fierce flame, the red, cruel coal, shall devour the doomed man, and his parting from life comes swiftly. The woman weeps when she sees the flames cover her child.
For one, a sword's edge on the mead-bench takes away his life: an angry ale-drinker, a man sated with wine. His words were too hasty before.
One shall become a man drunk on mead at the beer-drinking, through the cupbearer's hand. Then he cannot set a measure for his mouth with his mind, but shall lose his life most wretchedly,
suffer grievous harm, cut off from joys. Men will call him a self-slayer, and speak with their mouths of the mead-drunk man's drinking.
to live in days of joy and receive wealth, treasures and the mead-cup among his kin, as far as any man may hold on to them from then on.

So variously does the mighty Lord deal out to all across the surface of the earth. He apportions and decrees and keeps hold of the fates: to one prosperity, to one a share of hardships, to one the gladness of youth,
For one, wondrous gifts are made ready through the goldsmith's craft. Very often he, the mighty king's man, hardens and adorns well, and he gives him broad land as a reward. He receives it gladly.
